questions.question: Which of the following p-block elements is a metalloid?

solution.key_concept: The p-block metalloids lie along the diagonal: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te.
steps: The metalloids of the p-block are B, Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te.
Ge is in this list, so it is a metalloid.
Al, Pb and Bi lie at the lower left of the block and are metals.
solution.why_not_others: Al (Group 13), Pb (Group 14) and Bi (Group 15) are all metals.
solution.common_trap: Assuming Bi is a metalloid because As and Sb above it are metalloids.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember the diagonal B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te.

questions.question: Which of the following sets contains only metalloids?

solution.key_concept: The metalloids are B, Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te. Al, Ga, In, Tl, Sn, Pb, Bi and Po are metals.
steps: Check each set for a metal.
B, Si, As and Te are all metalloids.
Each of the other sets contains at least one metal.
solution.why_not_others: Al is a metal in set (2). Sn is a metal in set (3). Bi and Po are metals in set (4).
solution.common_trap: Treating Sn as a metalloid because it lies just below Ge.
solution.time_saving_tip: Spot one metal in a set to eliminate it quickly.

questions.question: A p-block element X has five electrons in its valence shell (ns plus np) and is a metal. X is

solution.key_concept: Group number = 10 + number of valence electrons. In Group 15, N and P are non-metals, As and Sb are metalloids and Bi is a metal.
steps: Group number = 10 + 5 = 15.
In Group 15, N and P are non-metals.
As and Sb are metalloids.
Bi is the metal of the group.
solution.why_not_others: N and P are non-metals. Sb is a metalloid.
solution.common_trap: Picking Sb because it lies low in the group, although it is only a metalloid.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: In the p-block, metallic character increases across a period from Group 13 to Group 17.
statements.R: In the p-block, non-metals cluster at the upper right while metals lie at the lower left.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Metallic character increases down a group and decreases across a period.
steps: Metallic character decreases across a period, so A is false.
Non-metals cluster at the upper right and metals at the lower left, so R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: Options (1), (2) and (3) all require A to be true, but A is false.
solution.common_trap: Reversing the trend across a period with the trend down a group.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In Group 15, N and P are non-metals, As and Sb are metalloids and Bi is a metal.
statements.II: In Group 14, Si, Ge and Sn are metalloids while only Pb is a metal.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: This tests how character changes within Groups 14 and 15.
steps: Statement I matches the classification of Group 15, so it is correct.
In Group 14, C is a non-metal, Si and Ge are metalloids, and both Sn and Pb are metals.
Statement II wrongly calls Sn a metalloid, so it is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement I is correct, which rules out options (2) and (4). Statement II is incorrect, which rules out option (1).
solution.common_trap: Counting Sn among the metalloids.

questions.question: The general valence shell electronic configuration of the chalcogens (Group 16) is

solution.key_concept: Number of p-electrons = group number − 12.
steps: For Group 16, the number of p-electrons is 16 − 12 = 4.
The configuration is therefore $ns^2np^4$.
solution.why_not_others: $ns^2np^2$ belongs to Group 14, $ns^2np^3$ to Group 15 and $ns^2np^6$ to Group 18.
solution.common_trap: Using group − 10, which counts all valence electrons, as the number of p-electrons.

questions.question: Which of the following elements has a filled $4f^{14}$ subshell in its core?

solution.key_concept: From period 6 onwards, p-block elements have a filled $4f^{14}$ subshell in the core.
steps: Pb is a period 6 element.
Its core contains $4f^{14}5d^{10}$.
Ga (period 4) and Sn and In (period 5) have only filled d subshells, with no 4f.
solution.why_not_others: Ga has a $3d^{10}$ core. Sn and In have a $4d^{10}$ core but no 4f electrons.
solution.common_trap: Assuming every heavy p-block element contains f electrons.

questions.question: The correct ground state electronic configuration of thallium is

solution.key_concept: Tl is a period 6 Group 13 element, so it has filled $4f^{14}$ and $5d^{10}$ subshells before $6s^26p^1$.
steps: Tl belongs to Group 13, so its valence configuration is $6s^26p^1$.
As a period 6 element, its core includes $4f^{14}5d^{10}$ after [Xe].
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) omits the 4f electrons. Option (3) omits the 5d electrons. Option (4) is the configuration of In.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting the $4f^{14}$ subshell for period 6 elements.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Core contains a filled $3d^{10}$ subshell but no 4f electrons

solution.key_concept: The type of core depends on the period. N has a half-filled 2p subshell, and He is $1s^2$.
steps: Ga is in period 4, so its core has $3d^{10}$ but no 4f: A-II.
Bi is in period 6, so its core has $4f^{14}5d^{10}$: B-I.
N is $2s^22p^3$, a half-filled p subshell: C-IV.
He is $1s^2$ with no p-electrons: D-III.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps the cores of Ga and Bi. Option (2) swaps N and He. Option (4) mismatches Ga and N.
solution.common_trap: Giving Ga a 4f core because it lies below Al.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the electronic configuration of p-block elements are correct?

statements.A: Ge, As and Se contain a filled $3d^{10}$ subshell in their core.
statements.B: The number of p-electrons in the valence shell equals the group number minus 10.
statements.C: The highest oxidation state of Group 15 elements is +5, which equals the group number minus 10.
statements.D: Ga is smaller than Al because the poorly shielding $3d^{10}$ electrons raise the effective nuclear charge.
statements.E: Pb has only a noble gas core, with no filled d or f subshells.

options: A, B, C and D only

solution.key_concept: This tests core configurations, the formulas for p-electron count and maximum oxidation state, and the effect of poor shielding.
steps: A is correct: Ge, As and Se are period 4 elements with a $3d^{10}$ core.
B is incorrect: the number of p-electrons is group − 12; group − 10 gives all valence electrons.
C is correct: the maximum oxidation state is 15 − 10 = +5.
D is correct: poor shielding by 3d electrons makes Ga (135 pm) smaller than Al (143 pm).
E is incorrect: Pb has filled $4f^{14}5d^{10}$ subshells in its core.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) misses D. Option (3) includes the false B. Option (4) includes the false E and misses A.
solution.common_trap: Confusing group − 10 (valence electrons) with group − 12 (p-electrons).

questions.question: Which of the following elements has the most negative electron gain enthalpy?

solution.key_concept: Cl has the most negative electron gain enthalpy because the compact 2p shell of F suffers strong electron–electron repulsion.
steps: F is very small, so an added electron is strongly repelled by the other electrons.
This makes the electron gain enthalpy of F less negative than that of Cl.
Therefore Cl has the most negative value.
solution.why_not_others: F is less negative because of repulsion in its small 2p shell. Br and I are larger, so they attract an added electron less strongly than Cl.
solution.common_trap: Choosing F simply because it is the most electronegative element.

questions.question: The correct order of first ionisation enthalpy of the Group 13 elements is

solution.key_concept: Poor shielding by d and f electrons raises the IE of Ga and Tl.
steps: B has the highest IE in the group.
The $4f^{14}5d^{10}$ core raises the IE of Tl above that of Ga.
The $3d^{10}$ core raises the IE of Ga slightly above that of Al.
In has the lowest IE, giving B > Tl > Ga > Al > In.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): B > Tl > Ga > Al > In
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) assumes a steady decrease down the group. Option (3) places Ga above Tl. Option (4) places Al above Ga.
solution.common_trap: Writing a smooth decrease down the group.

questions.question: The correct order of boiling points of the Group 15 hydrides is

solution.key_concept: Hydrogen bonding raises the boiling point of $NH_3$ above $PH_3$ and $AsH_3$. However, greater van der Waals forces make $SbH_3$ and $BiH_3$ boil higher still.
steps: Van der Waals forces increase with size, so boiling points rise from $PH_3$ to $BiH_3$.
Hydrogen bonding lifts $NH_3$ above $PH_3$ and $AsH_3$.
$NH_3$ still boils below $SbH_3$ and $BiH_3$.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) reverses the size trend. Option (2) makes $NH_3$ the highest. Option (3) ignores hydrogen bonding in $NH_3$.
solution.common_trap: Assuming $NH_3$ has the highest boiling point because of hydrogen bonding.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.R: Down Group 13, the +1 oxidation state becomes more stable relative to the +3 state because of the inert pair effect.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: The inert pair effect stabilises the (group OS − 2) state down the group.
steps: The inert pair effect makes $Tl^+$ more stable than $Tl^{3+}$, so A is false.
R correctly states the inert pair effect for Group 13, so R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: Options (1), (2) and (3) all require A to be true, but A is false.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the group oxidation state (+3) is always the most stable.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In Group 14, the first ionisation enthalpy of Pb is higher than that of Sn.
statements.II: S has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than O.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Irregular trends arise from poor shielding by d and f electrons and from repulsion in small atoms.
steps: The Group 14 IE order is C > Si > Ge > Pb > Sn, so Pb has a higher IE than Sn. Statement I is correct.
The compact 2p shell of O repels an added electron, so S has the more negative electron gain enthalpy. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are correct, so options (2), (3) and (4) are ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Assuming IE always decreases down a group and that the first member always has the most negative electron gain enthalpy.

questions.question: Which of the following elements shows only the −1 oxidation state in its compounds?

solution.key_concept: F is the most electronegative element and shows only −1.
steps: F shows only the −1 oxidation state.
O shows −2, −1 in peroxides and +2 in $OF_2$.
Cl and N show several oxidation states.
solution.why_not_others: O, Cl and N each show more than one oxidation state.
solution.common_trap: Thinking O is always −2.

questions.question: Which of the following species does NOT exist?

solution.key_concept: Second-period elements have only four valence orbitals (2s and three 2p), so their maximum covalency is 4.
steps: B can show at most covalency 4, as in $[BF_4]^-$.
$[BF_6]^{3-}$ would need covalency 6, which B cannot reach.
Al and P can expand their covalency using vacant d-orbitals.
solution.why_not_others: $[AlF_6]^{3-}$ and $PCl_5$ exist because Al and P use d-orbitals. $[BF_4]^-$ has covalency 4, which is within the limit for B.
solution.common_trap: Assuming B behaves like Al and forms a six-coordinate fluoride.

questions.question: The maximum covalency that nitrogen can show is

solution.key_concept: Max covalency of a period 2 element = 4 (2s + 3 × 2p orbitals).
steps: N is a second-period element with only four valence orbitals.
It has no d-orbitals, so its covalency cannot exceed 4.
This is why $NCl_5$ does not exist.
solution.why_not_others: 3 is its common covalency, not the maximum. 5 is the group oxidation state, which N cannot reach as a covalency because it has no d-orbitals. 6 needs d-orbitals.
solution.common_trap: Equating the maximum covalency with the number of valence electrons (5).

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: The F–F bond is unusually weak

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: HF has an abnormally high boiling point

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Nitrogen exists as $N_2$ while phosphorus exists as $P_4$

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Absence of d-orbitals in the valence shell

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Lone pair repulsion between small atoms

solution.key_concept: Small size, high electronegativity and the absence of d-orbitals explain the anomalous behaviour of the first members.
steps: N has no d-orbitals to expand its covalency, so $NCl_5$ cannot form: A-I.
Lone pairs on the small F atoms repel strongly and weaken the F–F bond: B-II.
HF molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds: C-III.
Small N atoms form a strong $N\equiv N$ triple bond: D-IV.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps A and B. Option (3) swaps B and C. Option (4) swaps A and D.
solution.common_trap: Attributing the weak F–F bond to the absence of d-orbitals.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the anomalous behaviour of the first members of the p-block groups are correct?

statements.A: Oxygen shows the +2 oxidation state in $OF_2$.
statements.B: Boron forms $[BF_4]^-$, whereas aluminium can form $[AlF_6]^{3-}$.
statements.C: Boron halides dimerise in the same way as $AlCl_3$ dimerises to $Al_2Cl_6$.
statements.D: The F–F bond is stronger than the Cl–Cl bond.
statements.E: $NH_3$, $H_2O$ and $HF$ have abnormally high boiling points due to hydrogen bonding.

solution.key_concept: This tests the unique properties of B, N, O and F compared with their heavier congeners.
steps: A is correct: O shows +2 only in $OF_2$.
B is correct: B is limited to covalency 4, while Al can reach covalency 6.
C is incorrect: boron halides are monomeric, electron-deficient Lewis acids.
D is incorrect: the bond dissociation enthalpy order is $Cl_2 > Br_2 > F_2 > I_2$.
E is correct: these three hydrides are hydrogen bonded.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, B and E only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) misses E. Option (2) includes the false C and misses A. Option (3) includes the false D and misses B.
solution.common_trap: Assuming boron halides dimerise like $AlCl_3$, or that $F_2$ has the strongest halogen bond.
